claims.claim: George Slusser asserts that Le Guin's writing gives the reader precise prose rhythms, in contrast to SF identified by its icons.
claims.source: George Slusser, 'Le Guin and the Future of SF Criticism', Science Fiction Studies #53 (March 1991)
claims.quote: Le Guin gives us precise prose rhythms.

claims.claim: Jameson names Le Guin's world-building technique world-reduction, a deliberate thinning of reality by radical abstraction and simplification.
claims.source: Fredric Jameson, 'World Reduction in Le Guin', Science Fiction Studies #7 (November 1975)
claims.quote: an operation of radical abstraction and simplification

claims.claim: Jameson's abstract states that in world reduction omission functions as utopian exclusion.
claims.source: Fredric Jameson, 'World Reduction in Le Guin', Science Fiction Studies #7 (November 1975), abstract

claims.claim: Jameson attributes the effect of Karhide to the immense time span involved and the great antiquity of its science and technology.
claims.source: Fredric Jameson, 'World Reduction in Le Guin', Science Fiction Studies #7 (November 1975)
claims.quote: the immense time span involved, and the great antiquity

claims.claim: Richard D. Erlich identifies a point in Tehanu where how Therru knows Tenar has lied is hinted at but never explained, and calls it a gap left for readers to fill.
claims.source: Richard D. Erlich, Coyote’s Song: The Teaching Stories of Ursula K. Le Guin (SFRA digital book, 2009 revision), chapter "Earthsea Revisited: Tehanu"
claims.quote: a significant gap to be left or filled in by readers

claims.claim: A reader commenting under Sean Guynes’s reread of A Wizard of Earthsea describes the novel’s language as managing to be both semi-sparse and beautiful.
claims.source: AeronaGreenjoy, reader comment under Sean Guynes’s Le Guin Reread instalment on A Wizard of Earthsea, Tor.com, 2020

claims.claim: Sylvia Kelso states that rhythm, as opposed to scansion, eludes most contemporary critical frames and is not susceptible to ideological analysis.
claims.source: Sylvia A. Kelso, "Boldly to Re-Venture: New Writing on the Works of Ursula K. Le Guin", Paradoxa 21 (2009), pp. 7-22
claims.quote: Rhythm, as opposed to scansion, eludes most contemporary critical frames

claims.claim: Sylvia Kelso analyses the opening sentence of The Lathe of Heaven as four opposing blocks — two compound adjectives and two clauses — that echo the rhythm of ocean on beach.
claims.source: Sylvia A. Kelso, "Boldly to Re-Venture: New Writing on the Works of Ursula K. Le Guin", Paradoxa 21 (2009), pp. 7-22
claims.quote: four opposing blocks, two compound adjectives, two clauses

claims.claim: Sylvia Kelso analyses the Always Coming Home opening as a long opening clause that checks into shortening phrases and brakes to a heavy pause at a colon.
claims.source: Sylvia A. Kelso, "Boldly to Re-Venture: New Writing on the Works of Ursula K. Le Guin", Paradoxa 21 (2009), pp. 7-22
claims.quote: The long opening clause checks into the shortening phrases

claims.claim: Le Guin, quoted by Sylvia Kelso from "Collectors, Rhymesters and Drummers", said that if she could hold to the rhythms of the dragon’s flight the story told itself.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "Collectors, Rhymesters and Drummers" (in The Wave in the Mind, 2004), pp. 183-84, quoted by Sylvia Kelso in Paradoxa 21
claims.quote: If I could hold to the rhythms of the dragon’s flight
claims.page: p. 17, quoting The Wave in the Mind pp. 183-84

claims.claim: Le Guin's remedy for over-relied-on sentence structures is to vary the pattern and read the sentences aloud.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Navigating the Ocean of Story - Session 1' (Book View Cafe, 2015)
claims.quote: play around with the order of words, the connections of sentences

claims.claim: Le Guin recommends giving secondary-world information indirectly, by hint and suggestion, rather than as an expository lump.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Navigating the Ocean of Story: Session 1, Continued' (Book View Cafe, 2015)
claims.quote: Giving information indirectly, by hint and suggestion, can be fun to write.
claims.page: answer to Benjamin, on infodumps in secondary worlds

claims.claim: Le Guin states there are no rules concerning sentence length.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Navigating the Ocean of Story - Session 1, Part 5' (Book View Cafe, 2015)
claims.quote: There are no rules concerning sentence length.

claims.claim: Le Guin's replacement for a sentence-length rule is variety and appropriateness, each sentence's length suited to what it has to say.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Navigating the Ocean of Story - Session 1, Part 5' (Book View Cafe, 2015)
claims.quote: I suggest that you try for both variety and appropriateness

claims.claim: Le Guin grounds prose rhythm in the body, saying art depends on rhythms and body rhythms are what writers use.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'What Makes a Story' (c. 2007), ursulakleguin.com
claims.quote: art depends on rhythms, and body rhythms are what writers use
